clue.text: A few expect that will never happen

parts.note: a few means some
to expect, look forward to

explanation.surface: Only a handful of people anticipate something that is never going to come about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some hope!' is a British ironic retort meaning there is no chance at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The ironic exclamation dismisses a wish as having no chance, so it is an idiom for something impossible.

clue.text: Spring dip, say

indicators.note: say means as it is spoken, so we want a word that sounds like this one

parts.note: a dip is a sauce for dunking, which in a non-rhotic British accent sounds identical

explanation.surface: A quick plunge into a natural spring.
explanation.walkthrough: The pair only sound alike in accents that drop the R, as in standard southern British English.
explanation.definitionFit: A spring is where a stream rises, its origin or headwater.

clue.text: Chap that redesigned an area of New York

parts.note: a chap is a man

indicators.note: redesigning something rearranges it, so those words are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man who replanned a district of New York City.
explanation.definitionFit: Manhattan is the central borough of New York City, an island district of it.

clue.text: Arrogance shown by Hudson's first director

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of the name before it

parts.note: the initial letter
an auteur is a film director with a strong personal style

explanation.surface: A director named Hudson behaves haughtily.
explanation.definitionFit: Hauteur is haughtiness, a lofty disdainful manner, so it is a synonym for arrogance.

clue.text: Upset, whistle-blower about to retire

parts.note: to be put out is to be upset
a whistle-blower is someone about to inform, that is, about to grass

explanation.surface: An informer, upset, is on the point of leaving work for good.
explanation.walkthrough: To grass is British slang for informing on someone; the whistle-blower is cast as about 'to grass'.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting an animal or worker out to grass is an idiom for making them retire from active use.

clue.text: Street guide, Northampton's centre, displayed in pub in market

indicators.note: something displayed in a place sits inside it, so these letters go within the pub

parts.note: a bar is a pub
the A-Z is the London street atlas

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter, the only one kept here

parts.note: the sixth of eleven letters is the centre

explanation.surface: A street map and the middle of Northampton are on show in a pub at the market.
explanation.walkthrough: AZ plus A goes inside BAR: B(AZA)AR. The A-Z is the standard British street-map book.
explanation.definitionFit: A bazaar is an oriental market or a fund-raising sale, so it is a synonym for market.

clue.text: Jumping bail, a bishop (a fictional character)

indicators.note: jumping suggests letters leaping about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
the a inside the brackets, taken as written

explanation.surface: A bishop skips bail, though he is only made up.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket looks like an aside, but its a supplies the last letter and the rest is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ali Baba is the woodcutter hero of the Arabian Nights tale with the forty thieves, a storybook figure.

clue.text: Hurt master, holding hearts and diamonds

indicators.note: holding something means having it inside, so one letter goes within

parts.note: an ace is an expert, a master
H is the card abbreviation for hearts
D is the card abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: A card expert in pain while clutching red suits.
explanation.walkthrough: Hearts and diamonds use the standard card-suit initials; only the first is held, the second simply follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Ached and hurt are both past-tense verbs for feeling pain.

clue.text: International organisation embarrassed being on trial

indicators.note: in a down answer, one part being on another puts it above, so first

parts.note: red in the face from embarrassment
a cross to bear is a trial or burden

explanation.surface: A global body is shamed when it finds itself in the dock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On trial' reads as in court, but trial means an affliction.
explanation.definitionFit: The Red Cross is the worldwide humanitarian movement, a well-known international body.

clue.text: Vase held by mourner

indicators.note: the answer is held within the following word, running inside it

parts.note: letters two to four of the word

explanation.surface: A grieving person at a funeral carries a vase.
explanation.walkthrough: The funeral picture makes the vase a burial urn, so the answer is in the scene too.
explanation.definitionFit: An urn is a vase, often with a foot and lid, used for ashes or ornament.

clue.text: She departs on a French lake, one that's unspoilt

indicators.note: one part placed on, after, another means the later group comes at the end

parts.note: the French masculine word for a
a tarn is a small mountain lake
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
D is the timetable abbreviation for departs

explanation.surface: A woman sets off on a French lake, the one place that remains unspoilt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the woman and her departure after the French, lake and one pieces, so the clue's order is reversed. A tarn is a small upland lake, as in the Lake District.
explanation.definitionFit: Something untarnished has kept its shine and good name, a synonym for unspoilt.

clue.text: Wave coming over ship, fairground attraction

indicators.note: in a down answer, a part coming over another sits above it, so first

parts.note: a roller is a long swelling wave
a coaster is a ship trading along the coast

explanation.surface: A big wave breaks over a vessel, a thrilling ride.
explanation.definitionFit: A roller coaster is a looping railway ride found at funfairs and theme parks.

clue.text: What could be at each posh country house in Bordeaux?

indicators.note: asks what these letters could become, inviting a rearrangement

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
U means upper-class

explanation.surface: A question about what might be found at every grand rural mansion in the wine region.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A chateau is a French manor or castle, and Bordeaux wine estates are known by that name.

clue.text: Editorial about northern youth who drowned

indicators.note: one word goes about, around, another, enclosing it

parts.note: a leader is a newspaper's editorial article
N is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: A newspaper editorial reports on a young man from the north who drowned.
explanation.walkthrough: In British papers the leader is the editorial column voicing the paper's own view.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Leander swam the Hellespont nightly to Hero and drowned one stormy night.

clue.text: Cause a reversal of fortune in pitched battle with hunters

indicators.note: things pitched are thrown about, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: the two words taken as written; with is a joiner

explanation.surface: In a set-piece fight against huntsmen, the hunted gain the upper hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitched battle' reads as a phrase, but 'pitched' is the signal acting on the two words after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn the tables is an idiom for reversing a situation so the loser gains the advantage.

clue.text: Servant's dismal day dashing about

indicators.note: letters dashing about are scattered and settle in a new order

parts.note: both words taken as written

explanation.surface: A domestic has a gloomy day rushing around.
explanation.definitionFit: A lady's maid is a female servant who attends personally to her mistress, a kind of servant.

clue.text: What a ticket may show pair attending reserve game

indicators.note: attending means accompanying, so the parts stand side by side

parts.note: PR is the abbreviation for pair
reserve as coolness of manner, iciness
tag is a children's chasing game

explanation.surface: A couple's admission ticket is shown for a reserve-team match.
explanation.walkthrough: The ticket suggests a match, but it is the label on goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A price tag is a label giving cost, which is what a ticket on goods in a shop displays.

clue.text: Panicking, carrying out chicken

parts.note: running a business is carrying it out
chicken means cowardly, afraid

explanation.surface: Someone in a frenzy is carrying out a chicken.
explanation.definitionFit: Running scared is an idiom for acting in a state of fear or panic.

clue.text: Endlessly disparage a king, narrow-minded

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is cut off

parts.note: insult, with its last letter removed
taken as written
R is for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps belittling a monarch is being blinkered.
explanation.definitionFit: Insular literally means island-like, and figuratively describes an outlook cut off from others, a narrow one.

clue.text: Book put to one side

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to arrange in advance, as a table
second meaning: to keep back for later use

explanation.walkthrough: Book looks like a noun, but here it is the verb meaning arrange in advance.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both booking a seat in advance and setting something aside for later use.

clue.text: Bird seen in very large quarry

parts.note: OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize
quarry as a hunted animal, prey

explanation.surface: A bird is spotted in a huge stone pit.
explanation.walkthrough: Quarry suggests a stone pit, but here it is the hunted creature.
explanation.definitionFit: The osprey is a fish-eating hawk, an example of a bird.

clue.text: Game in which players need to draw an Ace

indicators.note: to draw something in is to take it inside, so these letters enclose the next

parts.note: the players in a play are its cast
taken as written
A is the abbreviation for ace in cards

explanation.surface: A card game whose players must pick up an ace from the pile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw an Ace' reads as a card move, but only 'an' is drawn into the players; the ace is tacked on at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Canasta is a rummy-type card game played with two packs, an example of a game.

clue.text: Unacceptable idea one rejected

indicators.note: rejected means thrown out, so that letter leaves the word

parts.note: a notion is an idea
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A thought that was turned down was beyond the pale.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing I from NOTION leaves the answer; 'not on' is a British informal phrase for unacceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is not on is a British idiom for it being out of order or not allowed.

clue.text: Helps when it's rough on board

parts.note: as means when, at the time that

indicators.note: on board means aboard a vessel, so the letters sit inside the ship

parts.note: on board conventionally means inside SS, a steamship

indicators.note: a rough version is a disordered one, so those letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone lends a hand when the sea is choppy aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Choppy seas fit the surface, but 'rough' just jumbles the three letters, which then go on board the steamship.
explanation.definitionFit: To assist someone is to help them, so assists is a plain synonym in the same third-person form.

clue.text: Toast tailor's new betting system

indicators.note: a new version of the words is a remade one, in a fresh order

parts.note: both words taken as written

explanation.surface: Raise a glass to the tailor, whose new way of placing bets has arrived.
explanation.definitionFit: A totalisator, or tote, pools all stakes and divides them among winners, a form of betting system.

clue.text: Tune from couple with no piano

indicators.note: with no means lacking, so the letter for the next word is removed

parts.note: a couple is a pair
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: A melody performed by two people without a piano accompaniment.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing P from PAIR leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An air is a melody or song, so it is a synonym for tune.

clue.text: Go after information defining upper classes

indicators.note: one thing coming after another puts it second in the row

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
a go is an attempt, a try

explanation.surface: Pursue the facts that describe the upper classes.
explanation.walkthrough: Go reads as a verb, but it is a noun meaning an attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: The gentry are people of good social standing just below the nobility, the upper classes.

clue.text: Sort of fire to make one relaxed? Yes and no

parts.words: Sort of fire to make one relaxed?
parts.note: surface reading: a cosy, welcoming blaze in the hearth that helps you unwind
setter's reading: the word also names military fire from one's own side, which is anything but relaxing

explanation.surface: A question about whether a hearth fire calms one down, answered ambiguously.
explanation.walkthrough: The same adjective fits a welcoming fireside (yes) and accidental shooting by one's own forces (no).
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective qualifies fire in the military phrase for shots from allied forces, and describes a warm, welcoming blaze.
